request.system:
You are the requirements analyst in a governed software delivery pipeline. You turn a product owner's requirement into a normalized engineering specification that the architect, coders and testers downstream will build from. You do not write code.

Your output is checked by automated gates and then reviewed by a human before any design or code work starts, so precision matters more than polish.

How to work:
- Restate the goal in one or two sentences an engineer could act on.
- List functional and non-functional requirements as atomic, testable statements. Keep the requirement's own ids (FR1, NFR2, ...) when it provides them; otherwise assign them. Do not invent scope the requirement does not ask for.
- Surface every ambiguity: anything an engineer would have to guess about (formats, limits, error behaviour, status codes, security posture). Include the requirement's own "open points" and any you find yourself.
- For each ambiguity, decide whether a safe, conventional default exists.
  - If it does, set `source` to "assumption", put the default in `resolution`, and explain in `rationale` why it is the conventional and low-risk choice. These become recorded decisions a human will review.
  - If the answer is a genuine product decision (who may see data, business rules, legal or compliance posture, anything where a wrong guess would be costly to reverse), set `source` to "unresolved" and `resolution` to null. This stops the pipeline until a human answers, which is the intended behaviour. Do not guess on these to keep things moving.
- Write acceptance criteria as observable behaviours (request → expected response), covering the main path and the important failure paths.
- `summary`: one line, e.g. counts of requirements and how many ambiguities were resolved vs. left open.
request.user:
<requirement>
# Bug report: links to some valid websites cannot be shortened

> Input to the orchestrator's bug-fix workflow. The service in `url-shortener/` is in use.

## What users report
Support has received several reports from users who cannot shorten links to websites that open
fine in their browser. Creating the link fails immediately with:

    400 {"error":"invalid_url","message":"url must include a host"}

Examples from the tickets:
- `https://müller.de/angebote` (a German shop)
- `https://例え.jp/` (a Japanese site)
- `https://my_site.example.com/page` (an internal-looking but public host name with an underscore)

The same shop works when a user pastes its address as `https://xn--mller-kva.de/angebote`, which is
how some browsers display it when copied. Ordinary addresses such as `https://example.com/café`
work.

## Expected
Any link that a browser can open and that the service's destination rules allow can be shortened,
and its short link redirects to it. The error message should not claim that a URL with a host has
no host.

## Constraints
- The destination rules must not be weakened: links to local, private or otherwise prohibited
  addresses must still be refused, whatever form their host name is written in.
- Existing links and endpoints keep working unchanged.

## Known open points (for the Analyst to resolve or flag)
- Whether the short link should redirect to the address exactly as the user entered it, or to an
  equivalent normalized form.
</requirement>

<clarifications>
A human answered your earlier open questions. These answers are binding decisions. For each, keep the original question wording, set `resolution` to the answer, set `source` to "assumption" and start `rationale` with "Decided by a human:". Make the requirements and acceptance criteria consistent with every answer. Raise a new open question only if an answer itself leaves something genuinely undecided.

[
  {
    "answer": "An equivalent normalized form, normalized only where HTTP requires it: the redirect's Location uses the host's ASCII (Punycode) form, and non-ASCII characters in the path and query are percent-encoded as today; nothing else changes (no case changes, reordering or removal of components). Link metadata (originalUrl) keeps returning the URL exactly as the user entered it.",
    "question": "Should the short link redirect to the exact address entered by the user or to an equivalent normalized form?"
  }
]
</clarifications>

<previous_attempt_feedback>
Attempt 1 was not accepted. Fix the causes below.

1 open question(s) were answered by a human (see <clarifications>); treat each answer as a binding decision.
</previous_attempt_feedback>

acceptance_criteria: Submit `https://müller.de/angebote` through the existing link-creation flow when permitted by destination rules → creation succeeds and returns a usable short link.
Follow the short link created for `https://müller.de/angebote` → the redirect Location uses the host `xn--mller-kva.de` and retains the `/angebote` path.

Submit `https://例え.jp/` through the existing link-creation flow when permitted by destination rules → creation succeeds, and following the short link redirects with the host in its ASCII/Punycode form.
Submit `https://my_site.example.com/page` through the existing link-creation flow when permitted by destination rules → creation succeeds and the short link redirects to that destination.
Submit the equivalent Unicode and Punycode forms of an otherwise permitted IDN destination → both can be shortened and their redirect Locations use the corresponding ASCII/Punycode host.

Submit a permitted destination containing non-ASCII path and query characters → the redirect Location percent-encodes those characters as the service does today, without other changes to URL components.
Read `originalUrl` metadata for a link created from a URL containing Unicode characters → it matches the exact URL supplied at creation.
Submit a prohibited local, private, or otherwise disallowed destination using a Unicode host or its equivalent ASCII/Punycode form → creation is refused under the existing destination rules.
Submit any of the reported, otherwise permitted URLs → the request does not fail with `400 {"error":"invalid_url","message":"url must include a host"}`.
Use a previously created short link and existing endpoints → they remain usable and resolve to the same logical destinations.

ambiguities.question: Should the short link redirect to the exact address entered by the user or to an equivalent normalized form?
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: this is the binding redirect and metadata policy. It limits redirect normalization to the specified host conversion and existing path/query escaping while retaining the exact user-entered value in metadata.
ambiguities.resolution: An equivalent normalized form, normalized only where HTTP requires it: the redirect's Location uses the host's ASCII (Punycode) form, and non-ASCII characters in the path and query are percent-encoded as today; nothing else changes (no case changes, reordering or removal of components). Link metadata (originalUrl) keeps returning the URL exactly as the user entered it.

ambiguities.question: Does “any link that a browser can open” expand the service's currently supported URL schemes or URL forms beyond the reported website URLs?
ambiguities.rationale: Preserving the current scheme policy is the low-risk, conventional scope for a host-parsing bug fix and avoids changing behavior beyond the reported website URLs.
ambiguities.resolution: Do not expand the service's existing URL-scheme policy. Apply the fix to the reported HTTP(S) website URL forms, including the Unicode IDN and underscore-host examples, subject to the existing destination rules.

ambiguities.question: Which IDNA processing profile should be used to convert Unicode domain names to ASCII/Punycode?
ambiguities.rationale: Browser-compatible host processing is a conventional choice for a service shortening browser destinations and helps ensure Unicode and equivalent ASCII/Punycode host forms receive consistent checks.
ambiguities.resolution: Use browser-compatible IDNA-to-ASCII processing for supported HTTP(S) URL hosts, and use the resulting host consistently for destination-rule checks and redirect Location generation.

functional.text: The existing link-creation flow must accept `https://müller.de/angebote` and `https://例え.jp/` when the existing destination rules permit them.
The existing link-creation flow must accept `https://my_site.example.com/page` when the existing destination rules permit it.
A successfully created short link must redirect to its destination with the host in ASCII (Punycode) form when required.

For the redirect Location, non-ASCII characters in the path and query must be percent-encoded as they are today. Do not apply other URL changes, such as additional case changes, component reordering, or component removal.
The `originalUrl` metadata field must return the URL exactly as the user entered it.

The existing destination rules must continue to refuse local, private, and otherwise prohibited destinations, including when a prohibited host is entered in Unicode or an equivalent ASCII/Punycode form.
A URL with a host that is accepted under the existing destination rules must not fail with `invalid_url` and the message `url must include a host`.

data.goal: Allow browser-compatible website URLs with the reported Unicode and underscore host forms to be shortened when they pass the service’s existing destination rules. Redirect using the agreed host and path/query normalization while preserving the exact entered URL in metadata and keeping existing links and endpoints working.

non_functional.text: Existing short links and endpoints must remain usable; the fix must not require changing endpoint interfaces or alter existing links’ logical destinations.

data.summary: 7 functional and 1 non-functional requirements; 3 ambiguities resolved, 0 unresolved.
